source.title: Interpretable Debiasing of Vision-Language Models for Social Fairness
source.authors: Na-Min An; Yoonna Jang; Yusuke Hirota; Ryo Hachiuma; I. Augenstein; Hyunjung Shim

page_placements.theme: Applied SAE latents are largely but not fully monosemantic; top-activation labels can misstate causal role

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether selected SAE latent neurons encode specific social attributes, using attribute-specific bias effects and top-activating examples. This refines the polysemanticity discussion, but it does not analyze the cited InceptionV1 neuron or test ordinary neurons across arbitrary inputs.
record.gate_note: The paper cites polysemantic neurons as motivation and reports results on SAE-derived social neurons. The reported general-task performance, retrieval and VQA results are not included unless they directly inform the neuron-specificity claim. Results cited from other studies are not recorded.
record.test_reason: This is a debiasing-method paper. It assumes SAEs disentangle polysemantic encoder features (citing Pach et al.) and uses SAE latents as a tool. It reports only its own method's bias and performance results. It never measures whether the original CLIP/LVLM encoder neurons are polysemantic, how common that is, what causes it, or whether canonical polysemantic neurons share one feature. Its 'specificity' results concern SAE latents chosen for social attributes, a related but different construct. They go under fits_no_version, not V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SAEs localize interpretable, 'monosemantic' social neurons whose deactivation reduces bias with minimal loss of general performance. They note intersectional leakage, especially in LVLMs, and that clean disentanglement may not hold for complex intersectional biases. They also say excessive SAE intervention distorts semantic representations.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Matryoshka SAEs to create an expanded latent representation, selects group-associated latent neurons, and deactivates them during inference; it does not reproduce the original neuron-visualization or feature explanation method.
record.method_sensitivity: Specificity varies with modality and attribute: the authors describe text-encoder gender neurons as more specific than image-encoder features, and report age–gender intersectional effects. The amount of SAE reconstruction mixed into the original feature is varied, though the paper discusses this mainly as a bias/performance trade-off rather than a measure of polysemanticity.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE latents in CLIP encoders, chosen for social attributes, mostly affect their targeted bias (Table 2). There is cross-attribute leakage: age latents lower gender skew 10.6 to 9.2; 40% of 25 age latents are gender-skewed. LVLM latents show lower specificity. Some latents mix in hairstyle or 'practice' concepts (Fig. 10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents from multimodal encoders can be attribute-specific, but often mix correlated attributes or unrelated concepts, depending on SAE training data and model.

record.peer_reviewed: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (venue stated in metadata); the text identifies the paper as arXiv:2602.24014v1.
record.problems: The evidence concerns SAE-derived latents selected for social attributes, not canonical original neurons or their responses across a broad input distribution. Several interpretability results are qualitative visualizations without numerical scoring. The quantitative specificity table measures downstream Max Skew effects, which are indirect evidence about feature meaning.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were included: the paper's wider debiasing and general-capability evaluations do not directly measure neuron polysemanticity or semantic specificity.

untested.parts: No analysis of individual vision-classifier neurons responding to unrelated inputs.
No language-model MLP neurons are studied.
No test of superposition as the cause; SAE expansion is used as a tool.
No measure of the share of polysemantic neurons across architectures or activation functions.
No re-examination of canonical polysemantic neurons; only SAE latents selected for social attributes.
No comparison of activation ranges or scoring methods for labelling neurons polysemantic.

record.verdict_notes: Polysemanticity is cited only as motivation, to explain why pruning original neurons harms general capability. All 'neurons' in the results are SAE latents. The reader's V6 'supports' and 'limits_scope' labels are removed: the study does not re-examine canonical polysemantic neurons and does not measure polysemanticity of the model's own units. Row value error: T2-race-a06-age should be 59.1, not 63.0.

versions.untested_parts: No test of individual vision-classifier neurons responding to unrelated image inputs.
No test of MLP neurons in transformer language models responding to unrelated tokens or contexts.
The study uses expanded sparse autoencoders but does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more features than neurons.
No test of polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when feature capacity is sufficient.
The study varies SAE expansion, data and modality, but does not measure the share of polysemantic neurons or compare activation functions or architectures for that outcome.
Tests selected SAE social neurons and attribute specificity, not canonical neurons such as InceptionV1 4e:55, their full activation range, or whether its cat-face/car/cat-leg inputs share a feature.
No systematic comparison of activation-range choices or explanation-scoring methods for classifying neurons as polysemantic.

relation.reason: It motivates SAEs by citing polysemantic neurons [61] and uses SAE disentanglement as a tool. Its specificity tests concern its own SAE latents, not the claim about original neurons.

tranche.reason: This is a debiasing-method paper that uses SAE latents as a tool. It reports only its own method's bias, specificity and performance results. It never measures whether the original CLIP or LVLM encoder neurons are polysemantic.

source_check.notes: Both rows are SAE-latent ablations in the CLIP ViT-B/16 image encoder, so linking them to no version is right. The 10.6 and 90.1 baselines are random-latent controls at alpha=1.0. The unmodified image-encoder gender Max Skew is 18.8 (Table 4, alpha=0), so most of the drop comes from SAE reconstruction itself.

statements.correction: CLIP ViT-B/16 image-encoder SAE, alpha=1.0, top-1 latent per group, Gender Max Skew: 10.6 with random latents deactivated, 9.2 with age latents, 10.5 with gender latents, 11.3 with race latents. Age Max Skew: 90.1 random vs 72.7 age. Race Max Skew: 57.6 random vs 43.5 race. Supp. C: 40% of 25 age latents are gender-skewed. The authors attribute this to age-gender correlation in FairFace. Text-encoder gender latents affect almost only gender bias (Fig 5).
statements.problem: Numbers are right, but the scope is too broad. The leak is shown only for the CLIP ViT-B/16 image-encoder SAE (Table 2). For the text encoder, the paper reports almost no cross-attribute effect (Fig 5). Also, image-encoder gender latents barely beat random on gender skew (10.5 vs 10.6), so 'mostly affect their target bias' fits the age and race latents only. And 10.6 is the random-latent control, not the unmodified model.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Selected SAE social neurons in CLIP image encoders; strongest attribute-matched effects and inspected top-activating examples
reader_labels.reason: Age- and race-neuron deactivation lowered the corresponding Max Skew more than random-neuron deactivation, and the authors report single-attribute top-activating images (T2-age-a1-age, T2-age-a06-age, T2-race-a1-race, T2-race-a06-race, T2-visual-purity).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Gender neurons and cross-attribute effects in CLIP ViT-B/16 image encoder; gender neurons in CLIP text encoders
reader_labels.reason: Gender-neuron effects on gender bias were small in Table 2; age neurons also changed gender bias, and age-neuron deactivation increased racial Max Skew at both alpha settings. Text-encoder gender neurons were described as more attribute-specific. The evidence supports selected SAE features as often interpretable, not universal single-job neurons (T2-gender-a1-gender, T2-gender-a1-age, T2-race-a1-age, T2-race-a06-age, T2-text-b16, T2-text-l14).
